detail.scope: Commercial-sector electricity sales and average price by state, as reported to EIA. Data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class, so this is a proxy for their load, not a measurement of it.

sources.name: ERCOT
sources.scope: Large generators with a full interconnection study requested, from the monthly Generator Interconnection Status report for Texas. Includes projects from study through commissioning.

sources.name: NYISO
sources.scope: Projects in the New York interconnection queue as NYISO publishes them.

sources.scope: Projects in the Midcontinent generator interconnection queue, all statuses as MISO publishes them.

sources.scope: Generator interconnection requests across the south-central US, all statuses as SPP publishes them, withdrawn requests counted separately.

sources.name: CAISO
sources.scope: Active generator interconnection requests on the California ISO grid, from the public queue report. Completed and withdrawn projects are counted separately.

analysis.body:
The five grid operators represented here — ERCOT, NYISO, MISO, SPP, and CAISO — collectively show more than 1.3 million megawatts of generation and storage waiting in interconnection queues as of September 1, 2026, spread across roughly 8,378 individual project requests. These are planned power plants and battery systems that have asked to connect to the grid, not data centers themselves, and most will never be built; attrition in queues is historically high. Still, the composition of what developers are proposing reveals where grid operators expect load to grow, and for readers tracking AI infrastructure, the gas and storage figures are the most telling proxies, since data centers require firm, dispatchable power around the clock and often pair utility-scale batteries with their campuses. Because each operator publishes its queue under its own rules and geographic scope, the numbers are not additive in any precise sense and should be read as signals within each region rather than as a single national total.

Texas, covered by ERCOT, shows the most striking gas-and-storage combination of any single operator in this snapshot: 76,751 megawatts of gas and 160,906 megawatts of storage are queued, together representing the majority of ERCOT's 440,018 megawatts across 1,797 requests. That storage figure alone exceeds the entire MISO and SPP queues combined for that fuel type. On the commercial electricity side, Texas reported 15,753 megawatts-hours of commercial sales in June 2026 at the lowest average price of the states listed, 8.66 cents per kilowatt-hour, which helps explain why the state continues to attract large energy consumers. Virginia, the other major data center hub in this dataset, recorded 7,770 megawatt-hours of commercial sales at 10.99 cents, while California showed 10,024 megawatt-hours at the highest price in the group, 27.33 cents — a spread that carries obvious siting implications for cost-sensitive operators. CAISO's active queue, at 71,682 megawatts across only 265 requests, is the smallest here by project count, with storage at 46,943 megawatts dominating that total, consistent with California's mandate-driven battery buildout.

MISO and SPP together add nearly 500,000 megawatts of queued capacity across 4,902 requests spanning the Midcontinent and south-central regions, with solar dominant in MISO and wind leading in SPP, though both queues also carry meaningful gas and storage volumes — 30,236 and 47,392 megawatts of gas, and 68,429 and 52,913 megawatts of storage, respectively. NYISO's queue of 319,095 megawatts is the second largest by megawatts despite having only 1,414 requests, but nearly all of it falls into the "other" category at 291,136 megawatts, a classification that reflects how New York reports offshore wind and hybrid projects, making direct fuel-type comparisons with other operators unreliable. The EIA commercial sales data, covering Arizona, California, Georgia, Illinois, Ohio, Oregon, Texas, and Virginia for June 2026, offer a partial demand-side complement to these supply-side queue figures, but they measure all commercial customers, not data centers specifically, so the relationship remains inferential. What to watch next is whether the gas queue in ERCOT advances through study phases into actual construction approvals, since that progression — more than the raw queued megawatts — would signal that Texas grid planners are preparing to serve firm, large-load customers at scale.
